title: A Private IRIS for States and Utilities
one_liner: A consortium of former EPA toxicologists that sells open, peer-reviewed health-risk assessments (nitrate, PFAS mixtures) to state agencies, utilities, insurers and courts.
customer: State environment and health agencies (multi-state membership), large utilities, pollution-liability insurers, state attorneys general, litigation counsel and muni-bond analysts. Agencies and utilities pay membership, and lawyers and insurers pay per project.
problem: Step one: EPA's Office of Research and Development, home of IRIS, was eliminated in 2026, and the nitrate cancer review has stalled since 2023. Step two: EPA cannot update hazard values, while the four PFAS limits proposed for rescission (PFHxS, PFNA, GenX and the Hazard Index) may leave states to decide. Step three: states, utilities, insurers and courts need citable, transparent assessments to set or defend limits, and no one supplies them.
solution: A 'systematic review desk' using pre-registered protocols, external peer review and open publication. First deliverables: a nitrate health assessment and a PFAS mixture assessment, each with a state-adoptable guidance value and a cost-benefit table. Sell expert testimony and state-specific screening levels as add-ons.
why_now: ORD's elimination has released a talent pool of experienced risk assessors at the same moment the PFAS proposals are in comment and the nitrate review is stalled. The 2026 rollback creates a patchwork of state standards.
revenue_model: Consortium membership of $75-250k/yr per state or utility group, $150-500k per assessment, and expert-witness fees.
non_obvious_insight: Government risk-assessment capacity is a public good that is now for sale, and the asset is credibility, not technology. The buyers exist because states, insurers and courts need someone defensible to cite. Independence (open protocols, multi-funder, no client-directed conclusions) is the product.
first_30_days: Recruit three to five ex-ORD or IRIS scientists and incorporate as a public-benefit corporation. Pre-register a nitrate protocol. File an independent analysis in the open EPA PFAS docket to build credibility. Pitch three state agencies and the state drinking-water administrators' association.

title: At-Home Feline Urine Lab via Smartphone
one_liner: A non-absorbent litter collection kit and phone-camera strip reader that flags early urinary, diabetic and kidney-related changes in cats and routes trends to the clinic.
customer: Owners of senior cats, male cats with prior urinary blockage and diabetic cats, sold through clinics; clinics running senior and chronic-care programs.
problem: Cats hide illness. There are 53M US cat households (39%), multi-cat homes are growing fast, and only about 2% of cats are insured. Urinary obstruction and kidney disease produce costly emergencies. Urinalysis needs a clinic visit and a clinic-collected sample, so it is skipped.
solution: Starter kit with collection litter, a tray, dipsticks and a calibration card. The app reads strip colors on-device, tracks trends per cat, sends clinic-set alerts (blood, protein, glucose, pH shifts) and offers one-tap booking. Later: a phone-readable specific-gravity attachment and multi-cat pairing with existing smart litter boxes.
why_now: On-device colorimetric ML has matured, and smartphone-read at-home urine tests already exist for humans. Vets have become comfortable with home-generated data through CGMs, and cat households are the fastest-growing pet segment, while clinics need reasons to see patients earlier.
revenue_model: $29-49 starter kit plus about $12 per month refills sold through clinics with a 30% clinic margin. Diet-company sponsorship and insurer wellness programs later.
non_obvious_insight: The industry keeps building smart litter boxes to infer health from motion and weight. Chemistry is a cheaper and more informative signal, and cats produce the sample daily; the barrier was collection and interpretation, not sensing.
first_30_days: Validate dipstick plus phone reading against clinic urinalyses on about 100 cats in 2 clinics. Build a minimal app with the calibration card. Sell 200 kits through 5 clinics and measure adherence and alerts that led to visits.

title: Lights-Out Receiving Network for Driverless Freight
one_liner: On-demand night-shift dock crews plus remotely operable gates and dock doors so driverless trucks arriving at 3 a.m. actually get inspected and unloaded.
customer: Driverless-truck operators and their shipper and receiver customers, distribution centers with thin overnight staffing, and brokers offering autonomous lanes.
problem: Driverless trucks run around the clock, but most receivers have no dock labor, yard checks or inspectors at night. The CVSA enhanced-inspection clearance lasts 24 hours and requires a trained inspector, and hub-to-hub handoffs leave 'hundreds of dollars' of human cost per transfer. The PrePass/Kodiak bypass integration is live only in Texas and Louisiana.
solution: Three pieces. First, a network of trained ex-driver and yard-tech turnaround crews for walk-arounds, sensor cleaning and trailer checks. Second, a $3-6k remote gate and dock-door kit so the AV can check in and get a door. Third, on-call unload crews, with everything dispatched from one app and priced per turn below the cost of a human transfer.
why_now: Aurora is exiting 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and targets 30,000 by 2030, California's driverless-truck rules took effect on April 28, 2026, and the Teamsters sued on August 5. Hiring retrained drivers into new roles also buys political goodwill.
revenue_model: $150-400 per truck turn, equipment lease or subscription for gate and dock kits, and a per-lane subscription for receivers.
non_obvious_insight: Autonomy shifts the constraint from driver hours to dock hours: the truck no longer sleeps, but the receiver does. The rent moves to whoever owns the human touch at the endpoints, and hiring displaced drivers turns opposition into a labor supply.
first_30_days: Pick one corridor where driverless trucks already run (for example Fort Worth to El Paso). Sign LOIs with 2 shippers on that lane for overnight receiving, recruit 10 ex-drivers or yard techs, build a simple dispatch app and target first paid turns within 90 days.

title: Robotic Pack-to-Cell Teardown for E-Bike Fleets
one_liner: A robot cell driven by a vision-language-action model that opens e-bike and scooter packs, tests every cell, and regrades them for low-cost storage.
customer: Delivery-app fleet operators, e-bike and scooter share operators, battery-swap networks and repair shops (pay per pack), with buyers of graded cells for stationary storage.
problem: Micromobility packs are the high-volume end-of-life lithium stream arriving now, while EV end-of-life will not dominate until after 2040. Manual teardown is dangerous and slow, so packs go to shredders at low value or sit in shops as fire risks.
solution: A cell with a robot foundation model fine-tuned on pack disassembly with force feedback. It cuts nickel strips, pulls cells, tests each one (IR and impedance), grades A/B/C, and repackages A-grade cells for stationary storage or tools. C-grade goes to recyclers. It starts as a manual-plus-robotic service in one city.
why_now: 2025-26 robot foundation models made unstructured manipulation tasks feasible, and e-bike fire scrutiny gives fleets a reason to pay.
revenue_model: Fee per pack processed, plus margin on graded cells, plus recycler payments for C-grade.
non_obvious_insight: Recyclers built for EV packs face feed that is 15 years late. E-bike packs are small enough that a robot cell amortizes quickly, and their cells are far from dead.
first_30_days: Contract with 2 fleet operators or a swap network in NYC or LA. Rent a bench with a fire-safe enclosure and cell testers. Process 500 packs manually to build the dataset and unit economics before adding the robot.

title: Proof-of-Hours for Medicaid Work Requirements
one_liner: A text-message-first evidence engine that helps gig, seasonal, cash and caregiving enrollees document the 80-hour requirement, paid by managed care plans and safety-net providers for each member retained.
customer: Medicaid managed care plans (revenue is capitation per member), FQHC networks, hospital systems and county health departments carrying uncompensated care. Not the states: federal law bars plans from determining compliance, but outreach and enrollee assistance are allowed.
problem: From 1 Jan 2027, expansion adults 19-64 must show 80 hours a month of work, study or service. CMS projects 2.3 million people lose coverage in FY2027, largely through paperwork failure rather than true non-compliance. Georgia Pathways enrolled only about 16,000 people against roughly 359,000 potentially eligible. Irregular earners (gig, day labor, home care, seasonal, informal) have no clean payroll record, and states mostly rely on payroll data that misses them.
solution: A multilingual SMS, WhatsApp and app 'hour ledger'. It pulls earnings from gig and payment platforms via consented bank or statement links, sends one-tap SMS attestations to employers and clients, and logs volunteer and caregiving hours via QR check-in at partner churches and food banks. It screens for exemptions (medical frailty, caregivers) and outputs the evidence pack in each state's format, with renewal reminders every six months. The member owns the data and the plan sees only consented status.
why_now: Nebraska began enforcement on 1 May 2026. CMS issued its interim final rule on 3 June 2026 defining verification and the 80-hour test, and states did outreach in mid-2026. The national start is 1 Jan 2027 with six-month renewals, and plans are amending contracts now.
revenue_model: A per-member retention bounty ($40-$120 per successful renewal) or PMPM of $2-$6 for high-risk members, paid by plans. FQHC and hospital subscriptions, and later state contracts for outreach.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is not over who is eligible but over who can prove it. Compliant-but-undocumented workers are a large share of those at risk. The party with the strongest incentive to close that gap is not the state but the plan or provider whose revenue disappears with each disenrolled member. Verified hours are a portable asset the member can reuse at every renewal.
first_30_days: Partner with one FQHC network in a live or early-start state such as Nebraska. Hand-run a pilot for 200 enrollees using SMS plus a form, and build evidence-pack templates that match the state portal. Pitch three regional plans on a no-upfront-cost, pay-per-member-retained deal. Get privacy and HIPAA review done before enrolling anyone.

title: Robot Bullies: Paid Adversarial Pedestrian Panels
one_liner: A vetted panel of paid 'difficult humans' who kick, block, crowd and confuse sidewalk robots and humanoids on a controlled test range, so robot makers find their failures before the public does.
customer: Sidewalk delivery robot operators, humanoid and AMR makers preparing EU conformity files and retail or warehouse pilots, city permit offices that want interaction evidence, and robot insurers. First buyers are the safety or field-ops leads at 20 to 50 mid-size robot companies.
problem: Robots fail on human behavior, not physics. In 2026 an Uber Eats delivery robot was kicked over in Philadelphia, and robots circled in confusion in Lincoln Park in September. Each robot costs about $2,500 to replace, and the backlash is turning into permit fights. Makers test with polite employees or dummies. Nobody sells honest, repeatable samples of teens, drunks, kids, dog-walkers and wheelchair users behaving badly around a machine.
solution: A rented lot or closed street block set up as a 'behavior range', with a library of scripted provocations (path blocking, tailgating, encirclement by six teens, camera covering, gentle-force shoves, darting child-sized mannequins, cane and wheelchair users, leashed dogs). Screened, consented, insured participants are paid per session. Cameras and force sensors record everything. The output is a report formatted for conformity files and city permit filings, plus a recurring regression-testing subscription. Later: an anonymized 'Chaos Index' that ranks robot models by how they hold up against human misbehavior.
why_now: Sidewalk robots are now numerous enough to cause visible backlash, with the Philadelphia kicking incidents and the Lincoln Park swarm video. The EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027. ISO 25785-1, the first safety standard for legged and actively balanced robots, is still a draft, so makers have nothing to test against. Humanoid pilots are starting in warehouses and stores.
revenue_model: Test days at $8k to $25k per protocol set. Annual regression-testing subscriptions from $120k. Rev share with certification bodies (TUV, UL) on referred test packages. Licensing of anonymized behavior data to simulation and model teams.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not test-track capacity. It is honest human misbehavior at scale, and no simulator or employee panel produces it. The moat is the clinical-trial-style infrastructure: consent forms, insurance, screening and a bench of reliable trouble-makers. Robot makers will pay more for a 16-year-old's creativity than for another simulator.
first_30_days: Rent a parking lot on weekends. Recruit 30 paid participants from campus job boards at about $30 per hour. Have a lawyer draft consent forms and buy $2M of general liability. Pitch one local sidewalk-robot operator or university warehouse-robot startup a $5k to $10k 'chaos day' with a written report. Publish a free 'Chaos Report' on the Philadelphia-style behaviors to generate inbound leads.

title: AI-Native Estate Settlement Firm Under Arizona ABS
one_liner: A licensed alternative business structure that runs uncontested probate and small-estate work end-to-end at a flat fee, with attorneys supervising agent-driven workflows.
customer: Families of decedents in Arizona with $100K-$2M estates (uncontested probates, small-estate affidavits, simple trust administration), referred by funeral homes, hospices, senior living communities and advisors.
problem: Hourly or percentage probate fees don't work for $300K estates, so many attorneys decline them. Families face 9-18 months (unverified estimate) and $5-20K bills, run by an overwhelmed executor.
solution: An Arizona ABS-licensed law firm using agent workflows for documents, court filings, creditor notices, asset inventory, accountings and distributions, with attorney supervision at ratios far above traditional practice. Fixed price ($2,900-$6,500) with a timeline guarantee, payable from the estate at closing, and one point of contact. Add-ons include real estate sale and tax return preparation.
why_now: Arizona has permitted non-lawyer ownership of law firms since 2021 and Utah runs a sandbox. LLMs are now reliable enough for supervised legal drafting, and Arizona has a large retiree population. The brief's estimate of $5T of yearly transfers is heavily weighted to the very wealthy, leaving middle-class estates unserved.
revenue_model: Flat fees plus ancillary margin on property sales, tax preparation and accounting.
non_obvious_insight: Hourly legal billing can't profitably serve middle-class estates, but a licensed software-first structure can undercut on price while earning better margins. The regulatory sandbox is both wedge and moat.
first_30_days: Apply for the ABS license or white-label under an existing ABS. Sign 3 funeral homes or senior communities for referrals. Run the first cases with a supervising attorney, and get counsel to review unauthorized-practice and fee-sharing rules.

title: Sell the Route, Not the Business
one_liner: A standardized customer-book sale with a retention earn-out held in escrow and released automatically from payment data.
customer: Owner-operators aged 58+ of recurring-revenue routes with $80-500k revenue (pool, lawn, pest, cleaning, snow, window, HVAC maintenance, small bookkeeping and tax practices), and 5-30 employee competitors nearby who would buy them.
problem: No broker will list a $150k-revenue business, so retiring owners walk away and customers scatter. Buyers can't verify retention and the parties fight over price. Search funds target $5-50M companies and nothing serves the sub-$1M tier.
solution: Package the asset as the recurring customer relationship, not the entity. The product supplies consented customer-list transfer, a standard purchase agreement, a pricing multiple on trailing recurring revenue, and a 12-month retention earn-out held in escrow that releases as Stripe, QuickBooks or bank data confirms customers still pay. It adds customer-notice and handover-ride workflows, a non-compete, and matching to nearby operators. SBA Express lender partners finance the buyer.
why_now: From July 2026 an SBA 7(a) can be combined with a 504 for up to $10M, which loosens acquisition credit. Payment data now makes retention measurable in real time. An aging owner cohort meets flat CPA supply on the bookkeeping side.
revenue_model: 5-8% success fee to seller and buyer, plus escrow and retention-tracking fees, plus referral fees from lenders and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: At this size nobody needs to find a buyer for the business, because the natural buyer is the competitor with trucks two zip codes away. Retention escrow turns the valuation argument into a measured outcome.
first_30_days: Choose one vertical (for example pool routes) in one metro. Broker three deals by hand through Facebook groups and route-broker forums using a lawyer-drafted standard contract and Stripe Connect escrow. Document time to close and retention, then productize the paperwork.

title: Heat-Number Vault for Water-Project Compliance
angle: Pairing 2: Manufacturing reshoring/tariffs x Water infrastructure
one_liner: A registry that matches mill test reports to heat numbers for every pipe, valve and hydrant, producing audit-ready domestic-origin binders for SRF water projects and tariff-tier evidence for importers.
customer: Consulting engineers, contractors and waterworks distributors on state revolving fund (SRF) projects, at $1.5-4k per project. Foundries and importers claiming the 10% US-melt duty tier are the second buyer.
problem: SRF-funded water projects need domestic-origin documentation (American Iron and Steel, Build America Buy America). Section 232 duties now hinge on melt-and-pour or smelt-and-cast origin, and CBP is auditing origin. Certificates are PDFs that do not match heat numbers, and reviewers reject packages. Small engineering firms have no tooling.
solution: OCR and match mill test reports to heat numbers and purchase orders. Flag gaps before submittal, generate the compliance binder, and keep a verified-origin record that can be reused for customs and loan disbursement. Add manufacturer-side badges for foundries with clean records.
why_now: Full-customs-value 232 duties began Apr 2026, with 10% for US-melted metal. EPA announced $7.2B in FY2026 SRF funds, and USMCA rules of origin are tightening after the Jul 2026 non-renewal.
revenue_model: Per-project compliance fee ($1.5-4k), subscription for distributors, and a verification fee for foundries.
non_obvious_insight: Water utility procurement already forces the domestic-origin audit trail that tariff and reshoring tools lack, and the same data proves duty tiers. One dataset serves both the reshoring and water markets, and nobody has connected them.
first_30_days: Pitch five small-town engineering firms and two waterworks distributors. Do three projects by hand with a template plus OCR at $1.5k each. Use the misses and rejections to design the matching logic.

title: After-Hours Shop-Lab Leasing in Shrinking Schools
one_liner: A booking and insurance layer that rents idle high-school shops, labs and classrooms to apprenticeship programs, trade schools and microschools on nights and weekends.
customer: Declining-enrollment districts (facilities and business managers) and tenants: apprenticeship sponsors (JATCs, IEC and ABC chapters), Workforce Pell training providers, microschool operators.
problem: Chicago has 135k empty seats and more than 1,000 schools closed nationally in 2025-26. Districts are structurally slow to repurpose buildings and closures are politically toxic. Meanwhile trade programs need labs with power, ventilation and benches, and building their own costs millions.
solution: Inventory idle CTE shops, labs and gyms by the hour (power, ventilation, accessibility, parking), a standard license agreement with liability insurance and custodial and security add-ons, calendar and billing, and matching to tenants. Rent hours, not buildings, to avoid closure politics.
why_now: The enrollment cliff is squeezing budgets. Workforce Pell allows 49% of instruction to be outsourced for apprenticeship-linked programs, and data-center-driven electrician demand is growing training capacity needs.
revenue_model: 15-25% take of lab and classroom rent (typically $40-120 per hour) plus insurance and custodial add-on margin; optional district SaaS.
non_obvious_insight: The politically feasible move is not closing or selling but renting the hours between 4pm and 9pm. The tenants are already funded, and the district only has to approve a license, not a school closure.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 districts each with an underused shop or lab. Sign one apprenticeship sponsor as anchor tenant. Draft the standard license and insurance rider. List the first 10 rooms and measure rent per hour.

title: Rights-Cleared 1929-1963 Corpus for AI
one_liner: Join scanned mid-century books, magazines and newspapers to Copyright Office renewal records to produce provably public-domain text for AI training, with libraries paid a share and spared the scraper load.
customer: AI labs, foundation-model startups and fine-tuning shops that need litigation-proof training data, plus library and archive partners who supply scans (buyer is head of data or general counsel).
problem: Clean training data is now a legal necessity, but the best public-domain corpus (Harvard's Institutional Books 1.0, 983,004 volumes, 242B tokens) is largely pre-1929 text. For US works published 1929-1963, copyright lapsed unless renewed, yet renewals were rare (a 1961 Copyright Office study found fewer than 15% of registered copyrights renewed). The registration and renewal records exist but nobody has joined them to scanned text at scale. Meanwhile libraries are drowning in AI bots and have no sustainable way to offer their collections.
solution: Take scans that already exist (Internet Archive, partner libraries, HathiTrust-style holdings). Match each volume to Catalog of Copyright Entries registrations and renewals (Stanford renewal database for 1923-1949 books; Copyright Office online records for 1950+), and exclude foreign works restored under the URAA. Output a per-volume rights dossier with evidence links and a confidence score. Sell dataset snapshots with a signed provenance certificate (and insurance-backed warranty as revenue grows). Offer participating libraries a paid bulk-snapshot mirror (S3 or rsync) so AI buyers stop scraping their sites, with a revenue share.
why_now: The Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (2026-09-27) claim executives knew mass book piracy was illegal. Harvard and OpenAI/Microsoft-backed public-domain releases show buyers want clean data. Creative Commons (Aug 2026) says heritage institutions need standardized 'prosocial conditions' for AI access, and some (the National Library of the Netherlands, Trove) have closed access.
revenue_model: Dataset licenses ($25k-$250k per slice or annual refresh), provenance certificate fees, revenue share paid to libraries, bespoke rights-clearance projects for publishers reissuing out-of-print titles.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for legal AI text isn't scanning, it's rights determination: a huge band of 1929-1963 US works is public domain because nobody filed a renewal, and it's invisible until someone does the record join at scale. Libraries currently do this by hand. Evidence: Institutional Books 1.0 covers 983,004 volumes and 242B tokens (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08300). Wikipedia notes non-renewed pre-1964 works are public domain, the 1961 study, and the databases that hold the records (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_renewal). GLAM-E Lab survey: 39 of 43 institutions (91%) saw traffic surges, 69% of those blamed AI training bots, 74% deployed countermeasures, and robots.txt was largely ignored (https://glamelab.org/products/are-ai-bots-knocking-cultural-heritage-offline/). Creative Commons Aug 2026 on institutions closing access (https://creativecommons.org/2026/08/19/open-heritage-in-the-age-of-artificial-intelligence/). Authors Guild briefs, HN 626 points (https://authorsguild.org/news/ag-v-openai-top-execs-knew-mass-book-piracy-was-illegal/).
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick a narrow, high-value slice (for example 1950-1963 US trade, technical and hobby magazines where renewal was nearly nonexistent) and download the matching Internet Archive scans and renewal records. Days 10-25: run a first 5,000-volume join, have a copyright attorney sign off on the method and the URAA exclusions, and publish a free 500-volume sample with dossiers. Days 25-30: send the sample to 15 AI data buyers and licensed-data startups and to 5 mid-size libraries for a mirror pilot. Target one paid pilot in 90 days.

title: Data Estate Broker for Main Street Closures
one_liner: An appraisal-and-brokerage service that finds, de-identifies and sells the operational exhaust (quotes, work orders, dispatch logs, inspection records) of retiring or closing non-tech firms to AI buyers.
customer: Owners, business brokers, insolvency practitioners and CPAs handling closures of small manufacturers, freight brokers, insurance agencies, energy contractors and engineering firms. The buyers are vertical-AI startups and labs that need real workflow data.
problem: Failed-company data is now valuable. Google bought bankrupt Spirit Airlines' data for $10M: 100M emails, 30M+ recorded calls, 763,000+ flights of ops data, 1.2M fuel slips and 787,452 parts purchases. Mercor was the underbidder. But SimpleClosure, the main shutdown broker, only serves VC-backed startups, whose H1 2026 shutdowns were 27.3% B2B SaaS and 14.4% AI. Buyers say they want scarce data from manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services and logistics. Those firms close or retire constantly and have nobody to appraise or sell their data.
solution: Start with operational, non-consumer-PII data, which is the least legally fraught. Examples are work orders, quotes and bids, dispatch and routing logs, inspection and maintenance records, CAD revision histories, and internal Q&A threads. Run a 'data asset scan' ($500-1,500, credited against fees), then rights review and de-identification. Package the results as licensed corpora, run a sealed-bid sale to vertical-AI buyers and take a 25-35% success fee. Recruit business brokers, liquidators and trade associations as referral partners. Consumer call recordings and customer emails are excluded until counsel signs off.
why_now: Buyers proved a price in Aug 2026 (Spirit, $10M) and there is a losing bidder waiting. SimpleClosure's own asset report shows buyers paying tens to hundreds of thousands for unique corpora and wanting 'how real work actually got done.' Vertical AI agents for trades and logistics need training data that does not exist on the open web. Small-business retirements are a multi-year wave, and Sherline Tools going out of business (Sept 2026) is one example.
revenue_model: 25-35% success fee on data licence sales, plus a $500-1,500 appraisal fee credited against it. Optional recurring 'living licence' fees for firms that stay open.
non_obvious_insight: The market for dead-company data exists, but the only broker is aimed at software startups, while buyers explicitly want boring industries. Evidence: Google's $10M Spirit purchase with Mercor as underbidder (https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/18/google-buys-crashed-airline-spirits-data-at-auction-because-ai/5288962). The HN discussion notes that Scale, Surge and Mercor are recreating workplace data (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49343559). SimpleClosure's asset report lists 'manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services, logistics' as scarce-data buyers (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/what-your-assets-are-worth/). Its H1 2026 report shows its funnel is startups (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/state-of-shutdowns-h1-2026/). The main risk is privacy backlash. HN commenters doubt the de-identification ('I'm skeptical it'll be wiped correctly'), so the wedge is operational data with no consumer PII.
first_30_days: Week 1: pick two verticals, for example machine shops and freight brokerage. Book 20 calls with business brokers and CPAs who handle closures. Weeks 2-3: sign 3 exclusive listing agreements on a free data-asset scan. Line up 5 buyer LOIs from vertical-AI startups building quoting or dispatch agents. Week 4: complete one appraisal, get a privacy-counsel template for rights review, and run the first sealed-bid process.

title: Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral third party installs pre-construction sensors around proposed data centers and administers a developer-funded, automatic payout guarantee to neighbors, so permit fights run on evidence.
customer: Independent and mid-size data center developers seeking 50-500 MW campus approvals in contested counties. County commissions and state regulators are a second buyer because they can make the service a permit condition. Hyperscalers with in-house community teams are not the target.
problem: Permit fights are evidence-poor. Nobody has a pre-construction baseline of well levels, night-time noise, air quality or voltage at homes, so every later complaint about dry wells or a hum can be neither proven nor disproven. Both sides fight on feelings and lawyers. Politics has turned: New York paused environmental permits for data centers of 50 MW or more in July 2026, Texas ordered its environmental regulator to stop issuing new data center permits in September 2026, and local pauses now exist in at least 14 states. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 14% of Americans would welcome one nearby.
solution: Baseline-in-a-Box. Over 60-90 days before the application, deploy 30-60 low-cost sensors: property-line night noise, depth and conductivity in volunteer neighbors' wells, PM2.5, night-sky brightness, and voltage sag at homes. Publish a read-only public dashboard. Have a university extension hydrogeologist and an acoustician review the methods. Escrow the data with hash-anchored timestamps so neither side can edit it. Keep monitoring for 10 years. Then add a Neighbor Guarantee: a developer-funded escrow that pays affected households automatically, like parametric crop insurance, when verified well drawdown or noise exceedances occur. No lawsuit is needed.
why_now: In 2026 the moratorium movement jumped from town boards to governors' offices (New York's executive order of July 14, Texas's TCEQ permit halt of September 21). Developers now need social license as much as megawatts, and regulators are actively drafting the frameworks that will say what evidence counts.
revenue_model: The developer pays $75-150k per site for setup, $4-10k per month for monitoring, and an 8-10% administration fee on the guarantee escrow. Counties that write the service into permit conditions create repeat demand. Later, anonymized data licensing to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The baseline protects the developer more than the opponents. It is the only defense against future exaggerated or mistaken claims, and it turns 'trust us' into 'audit us'. Parametric payouts replace adversarial claims, which is why a rational developer buys it from a neutral party rather than opposing it.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a pending rezoning hearing (Georgia, Virginia, Indiana, Pennsylvania or Texas). Offer the developer's land agent a free 30-day pilot on 10 neighbor wells with an agricultural-extension partner. Build nodes from off-the-shelf parts at about $1.5-3k each. Present the live dashboard at the public hearing and convert that developer to a paid contract. Use the result as the case study for the next 5 developers.

title: Presence Ledger: Reconstruct Every Trip You Took
one_liner: Ingests flight emails, CBP I-94 history, location exports and passport stamps to produce an evidence-backed, officer-proof travel table for naturalization, green-card retention and tax residency.
customer: Immigration law firms (per-client fee), CPAs and tax preparers serving foreign nationals (Form 8843/substantial presence test), HR mobility teams, and green card holders or naturalization applicants directly.
problem: N-400 applicants must list every trip of 24 hours or more in the past 5 years with exact dates. Almost no one can. Officers compare the list with CBP entry and exit records, and an honest gap or mismatch turns an interview into a good-moral-character or false-testimony problem. Green card holders with long absences risk a presumption of broken continuous residence, and scrutiny of returning residents at ports of entry has risen. The same reconstruction is needed for IRS substantial presence day counts, state tax residency audits, and Schengen/UK day counts. Paralegals spend 1-3 hours per client pulling this together by hand, and it is still wrong.
solution: A consent-based tool that pulls the official CBP I-94 travel history, scans Gmail/Outlook for airline and hotel confirmations, ingests Google Timeline or phone location exports and card transactions, and OCRs photos of passport stamps. It reconciles them into a single timeline with confidence flags, asks the user only about unresolved gaps, and exports (a) an N-400-style trip table with the proof behind each row, (b) day counts for physical presence, substantial presence and Schengen limits, and (c) a warning when a planned trip would cross a risk threshold (for example 180 days, or a trip that would break continuous residence).
why_now: Naturalization is being scrutinized more heavily in 2025-26, with a new civics test, a renewed focus on good moral character and reinstated neighborhood-style inquiries. Border stops of returning residents are up. Remote and hybrid work has multiplied cross-border days and tax exposure. Location data is now easy to export from phones, and LLMs make email and stamp parsing cheap enough for a small team to build in weeks.
revenue_model: $49-79 per case billed to law firms (white-label), $29-49 self-serve for applicants, $12-20 per client for CPAs during tax season, and a $9/month subscription for green card holders who want ongoing day tracking and pre-trip risk checks.
non_obvious_insight: The danger is not the trips you forget but the mismatch between your list and what the government already holds. A trip table with attached proof, pre-reconciled against CBP's own record, changes the tone of an interview. The exact same dataset is what tax audits and residency disputes need, so an immigration wedge opens a much larger tax-residency market with no extra data collection.
first_30_days: Build only the N-400 5-year trip table with I-94 history import plus email parsing. Give it free to 10 immigration firms in exchange for a testimonial and a comparison against their manual tables. Charge $49 from client number 11 on. Post the before/after error rates from real cases. In parallel, offer a $15 8843/substantial-presence day-count report through 5 CPAs who serve OPT/H-1B clients.

title: Compute-Heated Housing: GPUs as the Boiler Room
one_liner: Put a liquid-cooled AI rack in an apartment tower's mechanical room and use its waste heat as the building's hot-water plant, cutting utility costs while hosting power-starved compute.
customer: Owners of 200-500 unit towers or planned conversions with central hot-water plants, especially in cities with building-emissions caps, paired with inference and neocloud operators seeking power and cooling.
problem: 20.7% of renters cannot pay utilities in full, gas boilers face per-ton fines under building-performance laws (NYC Local Law 97 tightens in 2030), and AI compute is starved for sites with power and cooling.
solution: Install one direct-liquid-cooled rack (about 100-130 kW) in the mechanical room. Capture waste heat, lift it with heat pumps to domestic hot water, and sell the building heat at a discount to gas or provide it free in exchange for hosting. The compute operator pays colocation rent, and we own design, integration and the thermal contract. Later expand to space heating and whole conversions.
why_now: Dense liquid-cooled racks produce capturable heat, AI power scarcity is acute, heat-pump hot water is mature, and building-emissions caps are tightening.
revenue_model: Heat-as-a-service at 30-40% of avoided energy cost, hosting margin share, and $25-50K design fees per building.
non_obvious_insight: By rough engineering estimate, a 300-unit building's average hot-water load (about 100-120 kW thermal) roughly equals one AI rack's heat output. The boiler room can host compute that cannot be sited elsewhere, and hot-water demand never sleeps. Precedents exist in Europe (data-furnace heaters and pool heating).
first_30_days: Run feasibility on five NYC and Chicago buildings with emissions-cap exposure. Get a letter of intent from one inference host for a 100 kW pilot. Sell three paid feasibility studies at $10-15K and line up host-funded pilot capex.

title: Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion
one_liner: A completion contractor that takes half-built solar jobs abandoned by bankrupt installers all the way to permission-to-operate, and is paid by the lenders whose loans go bad while the system sits dark.
customer: Solar loan originators and servicers, and TPO sponsors, that now hold stranded projects. The seven finance partners named in the Freedom Forever order are the first buyers: GoodLeap, EnFin, Credit Human, EverBright, Participate, Project Solar and Sunrun. Credit unions and ABS trustees holding 2023-2025 solar loans are the second wave. Homeowners are the beneficiary but do not pay.
problem: When a big installer dies, thousands of systems are left installed but not energized, or half-built. Freedom Forever went Chapter 11 in April 2026 and converted to Chapter 7 on Aug 7, 2026, with about 1,600 layoffs. The borrower stops paying a $30-50k loan on a roof that produces nothing. Lender, homeowner and dead installer each say it is someone else's job. The court let lenders hire new contractors and push systems to PTO, but a lender has no bench of crews and no playbook for doing it.
solution: Run the work as a records-recovery business first and a crew business second. For each stranded job, build a forensic pack: the AHJ permit file, the utility interconnection record, the design set from the dead company's design and CRM tools, equipment serials from distributors and consignment records, and a site photo audit. Sort jobs into tiers: paperwork-only (contractor of record and engineer's stamp need re-issuing), inspection fix, missing hardware, and never started (unwind and refund path). Price each tier at a fixed fee plus a bonus at PTO, and subcontract the labor to licensed local electricians and laid-off installer crews. Give the lender a dashboard of its whole stranded book with cost to cure and expected PTO date.
why_now: Freedom Forever's Chapter 7 conversion (Aug 2026, creditor claims due Oct 16, 2026) and the court order letting financiers step in make this concrete now. Sunnova (June 2025), SunPower (Aug 2024) and 100+ other solar failures came before it. Post-25D volume is down in 2026, so more failures are likely. Lenders have step-in rights but no operating capacity.
revenue_model: Fixed completion fee of $1.5-4k per job by tier, plus a $500 success bonus at PTO, paid by the lender or servicer. Add a monthly stranded-book dashboard subscription. Later, sell a 12-month workmanship warranty on completed jobs, paid by the lender, and a retainer for standby capacity when the next installer fails.
non_obvious_insight: A stranded job is 80% a records and legal-standing problem, not a labor problem. Permits, interconnection applications, engineer stamps and design files sit in a dead contractor's name and portal logins, so nobody can legally finish even though laid-off crews are cheap and plentiful. Also, the buyer is the lender and not the homeowner. The lender's collateral is worthless while the system is dark, it already has contractual step-in rights, and outsiders assume the homeowner is the customer.
first_30_days: Message loss-mitigation and installer-failure leads at 3-4 lenders. Use former installer ops people on LinkedIn to get the introductions. Offer to complete 10 stranded jobs in one metro at cost-plus, with payment on PTO. Recruit 3 laid-off project managers or permit coordinators and 1-2 licensed electrician subs. Write the per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer checklist. Target the first 10 PTOs inside 60 days, with case studies from them.

title: Harvest-Season Fab Van for Farm Machinery
one_liner: A trailer with industrial printers, a small mill and lathe, and a 3D scanner that parks at grain co-ops during harvest and planting and fabricates the broken part while the farmer waits.
customer: Row-crop and specialty farms, custom harvesters and independent ag-repair shops (Midwest, Plains, Central Valley), plus farm co-ops that host the van.
problem: A combine or planter is worth thousands of dollars a day inside a 10-day weather window. The dealer's part is backordered, discontinued or priced like a ransom. The failed item is usually a $3 plastic or steel piece: a latch, bracket, sensor mount, cab trim, bushing, pin, wear pad or knob.
solution: Two things. First, a mobile print-and-machine unit (carbon-fiber nylon printing, benchtop CNC mill and lathe, handheld scanner) that turns a broken part into a fabricated one in hours. Second, a growing digital parts library indexed by machine make, model and serial number, where every repaired part becomes a reusable file. Farmers can also buy a 'Season Pass' per machine that guarantees fabricated-part turnaround inside 24 hours.
why_now: The FTC and five states settled with Deere on July 8, 2026. For 10 years Deere must give farmers and independent shops the same repair software and resources it gives dealers, and it separately agreed to a $99M class settlement. That will grow independent repair shops, and parts are the next bottleneck. Crop margins are tight, so cheaper aftermarket parts sell, and harvest is happening right now.
revenue_model: Per-part fabrication ($40 to $600, with a rush premium), Season Pass subscriptions ($1k to $2.5k per machine per season), wholesale to independent repair shops, and a co-op hosting fee or revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: Farmers don't buy parts. They buy hours inside a weather window, so price against downtime avoided, not material cost. The scanned-part library by machine serial number is the compounding moat. Every emergency job builds the catalog that later lets you ship parts remotely, and the van is really a data-acquisition vehicle.
first_30_days: Borrow or rent a machine shop and start with two industrial printers, a benchtop mill and a scanner (about $40k to $60k), or begin with a used trailer. Sign two independent ag-repair shops and one co-op as hosts. Run a 'we fix it while you wait' pilot through the rest of this harvest, charging from job one. Post before/after photos in local farm Facebook groups and to elevator and co-op newsletters. Log every part as a file.

title: Corridor-Pivot Recruiting for Displaced Gulf Migrants
one_liner: When Gulf jobs disappear, retrain returnees and place them in Japan, Taiwan and Germany with the employer paying the fee.
customer: Employers in care, construction and manufacturing in East Asia and Europe that pay placement fees; the workers pay nothing.
problem: About $50bn of Gulf remittances is at risk. Returnees in Kerala, Nepal, Bangladesh and the Philippines carry recruitment debts and Gulf-specific credentials, and predatory agents will push them into worse corridors.
solution: A skills-credential wallet, language bootcamp and employer-paid placement pipeline, operated through a licensed recruitment partner. The wedge is care workers and welders from Kerala and Nepal for one Japanese or German employer.
why_now: The 2026 Iran-war energy shock displaced workers, and ageing economies are widening visa routes for care and trades.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k employer placement fee per worker, plus employer-paid training subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Displaced migrants are a supply shock nobody is organising. Employer-pays recruitment is both ethical and the direction of ILO fair-recruitment rules.
first_30_days: Sign one Kerala training institute and one overseas care-home operator, and run 30 candidates through a pilot.

title: MCP Connectors for Emerging-Market Government Portals
angle: AI agents & the agent economy x Emerging markets leapfrogging
one_liner: The maintained tool layer, with a human fallback network, that lets agents file taxes, e-invoices and registrations in Kenya, Nigeria, India, Mexico and Brazil.
customer: Bookkeeping and accounting SaaS, SME lenders, fintech onboarding teams and agent builders operating in Kenya, Nigeria, India, Mexico and Brazil.
problem: Agent tool ecosystems (MCP registries, Composio) index US SaaS APIs. In emerging markets the highest-value SME tasks, such as tax filing, e-invoicing, company registration and customs, live behind government portals with no API, monthly UI changes, captchas, OTPs and sometimes biometrics or paper stamps. Agent builders cannot reach 99% task completion, so agent products stall at the portal.
solution: Build and continuously test connectors (MCP servers) for Kenya's iTax and eTIMS, Nigeria's CAC and revenue-service portals, India's GST and MCA, Mexico's SAT/CFDI and Brazil's Receita and gov.br. Add a human fallback pool of cyber-cafe operators and licensed accountants who complete steps the agent cannot (consented OTP relay, captcha, in-person stamps). The buyer pays per successful filing, with a maintenance SLA.
why_now: The Ninth Circuit's 'the agent is the user' ruling and MCP's move to the Linux Foundation legitimize agents acting through user-authorized sessions. E-invoicing mandates (Kenya eTIMS, Brazil NF-e, Mexico CFDI, India GST) create recurring filing volume. Composio's $25M Series A shows the tool layer is fundable, and no one is building it for the Global South.
revenue_model: $0.50-3 per successful transaction, plus a monthly connector subscription per market ($200-1,000), plus a premium for the human-completion SLA.
non_obvious_insight: Connector maintenance is the moat because portals change monthly and nobody glamorous wants to own that. The human fallback converts 70% automation into 99% completion, which is exactly what fintech buyers pay for. The cyber-cafe operator, the old human middleman, becomes the agent's last-mile API.
first_30_days: Build Kenya iTax/eTIMS and Nigeria CAC connectors first. Sign three bookkeeping or SME-lending startups as design partners at a per-filing price. Staff the human fallback yourselves for the first 500 filings and log every failure type to prioritize automation.

title: Mother-Tongue Lifeline for Dementia Flashpoints
one_liner: On-demand live video calls where a dementia-trained speaker of the patient's first language and dialect coaches the English-speaking aide and calms the patient at bath, bedtime and exit-seeking moments.
customer: Home care agencies and PACE programs in immigrant-dense metros (NYC, LA, Miami, Chicago, Bay Area, Houston) with dementia clients whose aides do not share their language. Second: Medicaid managed long-term care and D-SNP plans. Third: families on a flat monthly plan.
problem: Bilingual and multilingual patients lose their second language as dementia advances and drift back to the language, dialect and idioms of their childhood. Agencies send whoever is available. The English-speaking aide cannot say the one calming phrase during the bath, so the bath fails, the patient panics, the aide gets hurt or quits, and the family blames the agency. Telephone interpretation lines translate literally, but a dementia patient's fragments and proverbs need to be validated, not translated. It is a communication problem, not an interpretation problem.
solution: A dedicated line, staffed on demand by trained bilingual retirees, nurses and teachers, covering the long tail: Yiddish, Haitian Creole, Toisanese, Cantonese, Polish, Russian, Uzbek, Punjabi, Tagalog, Greek, Armenian. A tablet or phone is propped where the patient can see it. The specialist speaks to the patient in dialect while coaching the aide in English in the earpiece: 'she's asking for her sister, say she is coming, then hum this song.' Sessions are 3-10 minutes at known flashpoints. Specialists are trained by aides in validation and redirection, not interpretation.
why_now: The post-war Soviet, Chinese, Caribbean and Southeast Asian immigrant cohorts who arrived in the 1960s-80s are now reaching moderate-to-severe dementia. Low-latency video is universal and cheap. AI companions such as KindredMind (voice clone of the caregiver, 12 languages, launched worldwide in May 2026) prove the demand, but they work best for mild cases and comfortable tech users. For moderate-to-severe dementia and live crises, the warm human voice in the right village dialect is the missing complement, and the agencies will pay per minute for it.
revenue_model: $1.25-1.75 per minute billed to agencies and plans, with 60-70 percent gross margin after specialist pay of about $0.45 per minute. Families get $129 per month for 20 sessions. Later, enterprise contracts with MLTC and D-SNP plans that cover the cost as a quality tool.
non_obvious_insight: Patients revert not just to a language but to a specific dialect and era, for example Toisanese, not Mandarin, and the idioms of 1955. A literal interpreter is useless because what calms is tone, a lullaby, a proverb and a familiar name. The buyer is not the family but the agency, which is desperate because language mismatch is why its aides quit its hardest cases. Nobody pays interpreters for companionship, so this talent pool of bilingual retirees is unmined and cheap.
first_30_days: Pick two languages with dense local demand, for example Toisanese or Cantonese in NYC and Haitian Creole in Miami. Recruit 10 bilingual retirees through churches, senior centers and community media. Train them in a one-page validation script. Run it on WhatsApp video with no software. Call 15 small agencies serving those communities and offer 30 free minutes per case. Sign the first three at $1.50 per minute with a $300 monthly minimum.
